target: AG1’s claim that a federal Election Day holiday would remove work/school scheduling barriers and increase turnout
objection: A federal holiday does not require most private employers to give paid time off, especially in retail, food service, health care, and other hourly or essential jobs. Low-income workers in those sectors may still have to work during polling hours, so the holiday would not reliably remove the scheduling barrier and could even leave the hardest-to-reach workers with the same problem.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would fail to solve the scheduling problem because many workers would still be scheduled
objection: Even if a holiday does not force universal paid leave, it still changes real schedules: many businesses close or reduce hours on federal holidays and schools are closed, giving workers at least some window to vote that they would not have on a normal weekday. So the claim that the holiday would fail to remove the barrier in any meaningful way is too strong.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would remove work/school barriers and reliably boost turnout
objection: The federal holiday would not mandate private employers—especially in retail, food service, health care, and similar sectors—to stop scheduling employees or pay them to stay home. Because many low-income workers would still face the same practical need to work during voting hours, the holiday would not generally remove the barrier; reforms that directly guarantee time off or reduce administrative hurdles are more reliable.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only helps if employers voluntarily give time off
objection: School closures and common employer adjustments on federal holidays mean the policy affects real schedules broadly, not just through voluntary paid leave. The objection is too narrow because the holiday changes school calendars and workplace patterns in ways that can create workable voting time for constrained workers.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday effects broadly give constrained workers time off or workable shifts
objection: A federal Election Day holiday does not require most private employers to close or provide paid time, so many hourly and essential workers would still be scheduled during polling hours. Likewise, school closures are not guaranteed everywhere and do not necessarily help working parents. Therefore the assumption that the holiday broadly frees constrained workers is likely false in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is insufficient because it does not guarantee paid leave
objection: If Election Day is a national holiday framed as a paid, non-work day, then voters get the needed time without losing wages or risking their jobs or attendance. That directly addresses the scheduling barrier for the workers most constrained by work schedules.

target: AG2’s claim that working on Election Day still leaves the same practical problem because people need enough time to vote
objection: The practical barrier is usually not needing the whole day off, but needing a workable time window. A holiday lowers the time cost by reducing ordinary weekday demands and making voting easier to fit around shifts, so the claim that workers would still face the same practical problem is too strong.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday creates workable time even for workers still scheduled
objection: A holiday does not guarantee time away from work for low-income voters. Workers whose shifts overlap polling hours may still have to choose between unpaid time, job/attendance penalties, or not voting, so a holiday does not consistently create workable time for the most schedule-constrained voters.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not create workable time because it does not guarantee time off
objection: A holiday also reduces the total time cost of voting by lowering traffic, commuting friction, and coordination burdens, since more family or community members are off school/work and can help with rides or supervision. So the holiday can make voting feasible even without universal paid leave.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reliably reduces travel and coordination burdens for low-income workers
objection: Lower traffic and more available helpers are not dependable for low-income, shift-based voters. Essential workers still commute, polling places may still be busy, and the people they would rely on for rides or supervision may also be working, so the supposed reduction in travel/coordination time is not robust.

target: AG2’s claim that holidays do not work in practice because workers still face schedule constraints
objection: International precedent shows the policy is workable: 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays. If holiday-based elections generally failed to make voting workable, that widespread adoption would not exist.

target: AG1’s inference from OECD countries that holiday elections prove the policy solves scheduling barriers
objection: OECD precedent does not show that holidays alone solve the U.S. problem, because those countries often have different labor protections, stronger baseline access to time off, and more voting outside Election Day. The international example may reflect other supporting institutions rather than proving the holiday itself reliably removes scheduling barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not meaningfully reduce the time barrier beyond work time itself
objection: The barrier is not just work versus no work; it also includes travel and waiting. A national holiday spreads voting demand over a longer day, reduces peak congestion, and makes it easier to fit voting around shifts, so the policy can still materially reduce the total time burden.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not help unless employers provide paid time off
objection: A holiday can reduce waiting time by increasing the number of people and volunteers available to staff elections, which shortens lines and lowers the total time needed to vote. That means the policy can help even if some workers still have to work.

target: AG1’s claim that election-day holidays are a strong turnout strategy because they address scheduling barriers
objection: Holiday status is a weak, low-yield turnout tool compared with reforms that directly remove barriers such as registration improvements, guaranteed time off, or expanded voting options. Research indicates a holiday by itself does not reliably produce meaningful turnout gains, and its benefits may mainly go to people who already have flexible schedules.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a minor convenience and not a major turnout reform
objection: The biggest barrier for many voters is practical time, not motivation. A paid, non-school/non-work Election Day directly gives people the time to vote, changes school and workplace schedules, and can reshape the broader civic environment around voting, so it is more than a small convenience tweak.

target: AG1’s claim that a paid, non-work holiday gives low-income workers the needed time to vote
objection: Federal holiday status does not compel private employers to provide paid leave or to stop scheduling people. In hourly and essential sectors, many workers can still be working during polling hours, so the supposed paid non-work day does not generally exist for the people most constrained by schedules.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday-based turnout gains are weak because the policy is mostly about convenience or attention
objection: The dominant barrier is limited workable time caused by work and school schedules, and a holiday directly removes that barrier by freeing time, changing schedules, and lowering the burden of voting. That makes it a substantive turnout reform, not a weak convenience measure.

target: AG1’s claim that turning Election Day into a paid non-work day creates needed time for schedule-constrained workers
objection: That claim assumes federal holiday status reliably produces paid time away from work for the people most constrained by schedules. It does not: private employers are not required to give paid leave, so many low-income hourly workers still face the same work-vs-voting tradeoff, including travel and waiting time.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is merely an attention/convenience tweak rather than a high-yield turnout reform
objection: A national holiday directly tackles the practical constraint that keeps millions from voting: work and school obligations. It also changes school, family, and workplace schedules, and can reduce congestion and waiting, so the policy is more effective than the target suggests.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday reliably restructures routines so schedule-constrained voters can find time to vote
objection: A federal holiday does not require most private employers to close or provide paid time off. In many hourly and essential jobs, workers are still staffed during polling hours, so the holiday does not reliably create usable voting time for the people most constrained by schedules.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday-based turnout gains are low-yield and mostly symbolic
objection: A holiday changes the real scheduling environment by closing schools, shifting workplace routines, and making more people available throughout the day. That materially improves access to voting for people whose main barrier is time, not merely attention, and therefore the policy is a workable turnout reform.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday meaningfully creates paid non-work time and school/childcare availability for constrained voters
objection: Federal holiday status does not require most private employers to close or give paid time off, especially in hourly sectors. Many low-income shift workers would still be scheduled during voting hours, so the policy does not reliably create the non-work time it depends on to increase turnout.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is a weak turnout strategy because it mainly changes convenience
objection: Election Day as a holiday is a strong turnout reform because it directly removes work and school scheduling barriers, lowers commuting and waiting friction, and increases the amount of usable time people have to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday materially reduces the time barrier for low-income voters
objection: A federal holiday does not compel most private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail, food service, health care, and similar sectors will still work during voting hours. That undercuts the claim that the policy reliably reduces the time barrier for those most constrained.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is mainly a weak convenience measure rather than a high-yield reform
objection: The dominant barrier is workable time, and a non-school/non-work day substantially loosens work and attendance constraints. This directly helps voters find time to vote, reduces pressure on schedules, and is supported by broad public backing and international precedent.

target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday substantially loosens work and school constraints for the most schedule-constrained voters
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or to provide paid time off, so in many hourly and essential sectors workers can still be scheduled during the voting window. That means the central work-vs-voting constraint remains largely intact for many low-income voters.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is not high-yield because it only gives people convenience and not real time
objection: A holiday is high-yield because it substantially loosens work and school obligations, changes childcare and community availability, and reduces the practical time cost of voting. It is therefore a direct way to increase turnout, not a symbolic convenience.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday substantially makes voting time workable for constrained workers
objection: A federal holiday does not force most private employers to close or grant paid leave, especially in hourly and essential sectors. So many workers still must choose between voting and their shifts, meaning the holiday cannot reliably convert voting into a feasible option for the people most constrained by work schedules.
